title: How the rook moves
outcomes: Taps every square a rook can reach, including captures and blocked lines
Predicts whether a line is blocked before moving
Says why a rook cannot reach a square that is off its rank and file

steps.text: That was a **rook**, the piece shaped like a castle tower. It slides in a straight line along its **file** (column) or its **rank** (row), one square or many, and never diagonally. Look at the next board: from d4 it reaches 14 squares.

steps.caption: All 14: the whole d-file and the whole fourth rank. The rook may stop on any of them.

claims.statement: These are exactly the squares the rook on d4 can move to.

steps.caption: A white pawn (the small piece that starts in front of the army) stands on d6. The rook reaches d5 and no further up: it cannot jump, and it cannot land on its own piece.

claims.statement: With a white pawn on d6, the rook reaches these squares and no others.

steps.caption: Make the pawn Black's and the rook may take it: it lands on the pawn's square, the pawn leaves the board, and the slide ends there.

line.say: The rook lands on d6, removes the pawn and stops.

claims.statement: The rook can move from d4 to d6, capturing the pawn.

steps.text: Before you move a rook, ask three questions. Is the square on its file or its rank? Is anything standing in between? If a piece stands on the target square, is it yours (not allowed) or the enemy's (a capture, and the slide ends)?

steps.prompt: Say it back in two or three sentences: how does a rook move, what stops it, and which squares can it never reach?

steps.text: **Compare.** A rook slides any number of squares along a rank or a file, never diagonally. It stops before its own pieces, and it may land on an enemy piece to capture it, which ends the slide.
